subject: biology
title: B2.2 Organelles and compartmentalization
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: B2.2 Organelles and compartmentalization — IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025), topic B2.2.
meta_desc: IB DP Biology practice covering B2.2 Organelles and compartmentalization, guide topic B2.2.
final_note: You worked through B2.2 Organelles and compartmentalization — 9 guide statements.

concepts.def: A discrete subunit of a cell that is adapted to perform a specific function. Organelles include the nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts, vesicles, ribosomes and the plasma membrane; an organelle may or may not be bounded by a membrane. The cell wall, the cytoskeleton and the cytoplasm are not considered organelles.

The network of protein filaments and microtubules that runs through the cytoplasm, giving the cell its shape and moving organelles and chromosomes. Although it has clear functions, it is a continuous framework rather than a discrete subunit, so, like the cytoplasm and the cell wall, it is not considered an organelle.

The separation of the components of cells so that the function of each type of organelle can be studied on its own. Cells are broken open in a cold, isotonic, buffered solution and the homogenate is spun in an ultracentrifuge at a series of increasing speeds: larger, denser organelles such as nuclei form a pellet at lower speeds, and smaller ones such as ribosomes only at very high speeds. Study of the function of individual organelles became possible once ultracentrifuges had been invented and these methods developed, an example of progress in science following the development of a new technique.

The nucleus holds the DNA of a eukaryotic cell inside a double membrane, and functional ribosomes are found only in the cytoplasm (ribosomal subunits are assembled in the nucleolus but join into working ribosomes only after leaving the nucleus). Transcription therefore takes place in the nucleus and translation in the cytoplasm, so newly transcribed mRNA does not meet ribosomes until it has left the nucleus, and it can be modified before that happens.

Changes made to mRNA in the nucleus after transcription and before translation, for example the removal of some sections of the RNA and the addition of protective groups at its ends. It is possible in eukaryotes because the nuclear membrane keeps new mRNA away from ribosomes. In prokaryotes, which have no nucleus, this is not possible: mRNA may meet ribosomes immediately and be translated while it is still being transcribed.

The division of the cytoplasm of a eukaryotic cell into membrane-bound compartments such as organelles and vesicles. Its advantages include concentrating the enzymes and metabolites of a process together in a small volume, so that reactions proceed rapidly, and separating biochemical processes that are incompatible with each other, for example keeping hydrolytic enzymes inside lysosomes apart from the rest of the cytoplasm.

A small membrane-bound vesicle containing hydrolytic enzymes at a concentration far higher than could safely exist in the cytoplasm, together with the conditions those enzymes need. Lysosomes fuse with phagocytic vacuoles to digest their contents and also break down damaged organelles; the lysosome membrane keeps the enzymes from hydrolysing the cell's own structures.

A vacuole formed when a cell engulfs material such as a bacterium or a food particle by endocytosis. Lysosomes fuse with the phagocytic vacuole, delivering hydrolytic enzymes at high concentration into a compartment where they digest the contents without acting on the rest of the cell; the products of digestion are then absorbed into the cytoplasm.

The folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane, which greatly increase its surface area. The inner membrane holds the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, so the large area of the cristae allows a mitochondrion to carry out oxidative phosphorylation at a high rate.

The narrow compartment between the outer and inner membranes of a mitochondrion. The electron transport chain pumps protons into it from the matrix; because its volume is small, a relatively small number of protons produces a steep concentration gradient across the inner membrane, which drives ATP synthesis by chemiosmosis.

The fluid enclosed by the inner mitochondrial membrane. The enzymes and substrates of the link reaction and the Krebs cycle are compartmentalized in the matrix at high concentration, so these reactions proceed rapidly, and the reduced NAD they produce is generated close to the electron transport chain in the inner membrane.

A flattened, membrane-bound sac inside a chloroplast, arranged in stacks called grana. The thylakoid membranes have a large total surface area and hold the photosystems and electron carriers of the light-dependent reactions; the small volume of fluid inside each thylakoid allows a proton gradient to build up quickly for ATP synthesis by chemiosmosis.

The fluid surrounding the thylakoids inside a chloroplast. The enzymes and substrates of the Calvin cycle are compartmentalized in the stroma, where the ATP and reduced NADP produced by the thylakoid membranes are used to fix carbon dioxide and produce carbohydrate.

The double membrane that bounds the nucleus, consisting of two phospholipid bilayers. It separates transcription from translation, is perforated by nuclear pores that allow selected materials to pass between nucleus and cytoplasm, and breaks into vesicles during mitosis and meiosis so that spindle microtubules can attach to and move the chromosomes, re-forming around each set of chromosomes afterwards.

A channel that passes through both membranes of the nuclear envelope. Large molecules cannot cross the phospholipid bilayers themselves, so pores are needed to allow mRNA and ribosomal subunits to leave the nucleus and to allow proteins such as polymerases and histones, and the nucleotides needed for replication and transcription, to enter it.

A ribosome in the cytoplasm that is not attached to a membrane. Free ribosomes synthesise proteins that are retained in the cell, such as the enzymes of glycolysis and other proteins that function in the cytoplasm or the nucleus.

A network of flattened membrane sacs, continuous with the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope, with ribosomes bound to its cytoplasmic surface. Polypeptides made by these membrane-bound ribosomes pass into the lumen of the rough ER, from which they are carried in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus. These are proteins for transport within the cell, for insertion into membranes, or for secretion from the cell.

A stack of flattened membrane sacs (cisternae) that receives protein from the rough endoplasmic reticulum in vesicles, processes it, for example by modifying the carbohydrate groups attached to it, and packages it into vesicles that bud off from the opposite face of the stack. Vesicles from the Golgi apparatus carry the protein to the plasma membrane, where it is secreted by exocytosis.

A small, spherical, membrane-bound sac that buds off from a membrane such as the plasma membrane, the endoplasmic reticulum or the Golgi apparatus, carries material within the cell and delivers it by fusing with another membrane. Vesicles are formed in endocytosis, transport protein from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus and from the Golgi apparatus to the plasma membrane, and release their contents from the cell in exocytosis, when the vesicle membrane becomes part of the plasma membrane.

A protein that assembles into a lattice on the cytoplasmic side of a membrane, causing the membrane to bend into a coated pit that pinches off as a vesicle. The clathrin coat is shed once the vesicle has formed, so that the vesicle can fuse with its target membrane.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly applies the term organelle as it is used in IB Biology?
options: The plasma membrane is an organelle, although it forms the boundary of the cytoplasm.
Ribosomes are not organelles, because they are not bounded by a membrane.
The cell wall is an organelle, because it is a labelled part with a function.
The cytoskeleton is an organelle, because it is a structure that moves organelles.
mcqs.specStatementText: What counts as an organelle, and how their jobs were found
mcqs.explain: An organelle is a discrete subunit of a cell adapted to a specific function. The plasma membrane is such a unit, controlling exchange with the surroundings, and the guide lists it with nuclei, vesicles and ribosomes as an organelle.
rationales: An organelle is a discrete subunit of a cell adapted to a specific function. The plasma membrane is such a unit, controlling exchange with the surroundings, and the guide lists it with nuclei, vesicles and ribosomes as an organelle.

A student who defines an organelle as a membrane-bound structure picks this. The IB definition is based on function: a ribosome is a discrete subunit adapted to protein synthesis, so it is an organelle.
A student who treats every labelled structure as an organelle picks this. The cell wall is an extracellular layer, not a discrete subunit of the cell, and the guide states it is not an organelle.

A student who groups any named internal structure with the organelles picks this. The cytoskeleton is a continuous framework running through the cytoplasm, not a discrete subunit, and is not considered an organelle.

mcqs.q: Liver cells were broken open in a cold, isotonic, buffered solution and the homogenate was spun in an ultracentrifuge at a series of increasing speeds. Only the pellet formed at the second speed consumed oxygen and produced ATP when supplied with substrates. What does this investigation illustrate about how progress in science is made?
options: Electron micrographs of the organelles in the second pellet would have revealed the same function, so the centrifuge added little that was new.
A technique for isolating one type of organelle made it possible to test its function directly, which could not be done before.
The ATP must have come from intact cells surviving in the pellet, since organelles cannot work once removed from a cell.
A single spin at the highest speed would have brought every organelle down in one pellet that could be tested just as well.
mcqs.specStatementText: What counts as an organelle, and how their jobs were found
mcqs.explain: Differential centrifugation separated a fraction rich in mitochondria, and that fraction alone respired. Study of the function of individual organelles became possible once ultracentrifuges and cell fractionation methods had been developed: progress in science often follows a new technique.
rationales: A student who thinks organelle functions were read off from images picks this. A micrograph shows structure only; oxygen consumption and ATP production could only be demonstrated by isolating the organelle and testing it, which needed the ultracentrifuge.

Differential centrifugation separated a fraction rich in mitochondria, and that fraction alone respired. Study of the function of individual organelles became possible once ultracentrifuges and cell fractionation methods had been developed: progress in science often follows a new technique.

A student who extends cell theory to mean that nothing smaller than a cell can carry out a process picks this. Isolated mitochondria in a suitable solution consume oxygen and make ATP; that is exactly what makes cell fractionation informative.

A student who thinks centrifuging merely speeds up settling picks this. A single high-speed spin would bring down every organelle together; only a series of increasing speeds separates nuclei, then mitochondria, then smaller components into different pellets. A mixed pellet could not show which organelle was responsible for the oxygen consumption.

mcqs.q: In a eukaryotic cell, newly transcribed RNA is modified in the nucleus before it is translated. How does the separation of the nucleus from the cytoplasm make this possible?
options: Ribosomes inside the nucleus translate the RNA while it is being modified, so the two processes run together in the same place.
The nuclear membrane keeps the ribosomes away from the DNA, which they would otherwise translate directly into protein.
Translation happens only in the cytoplasm, so the RNA cannot meet a ribosome until modified and out through a pore.
Modification of RNA before translation happens in all kinds of cell, so the nucleus is not what makes it possible.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why keep the nucleus and cytoplasm apart
mcqs.explain: Transcription takes place in the nucleus and translation in the cytoplasm. Because the nuclear membrane separates the two, post-transcriptional modification of mRNA can happen before the mRNA meets ribosomes, which is the advantage the guide identifies.
rationales: A student who places translation in the nucleus picks this. There are no functional ribosomes in the nucleus; translation happens in the cytoplasm, which is precisely why modification can be completed first.

A student who skips the role of mRNA picks this. Ribosomes translate mRNA, not DNA, so the membrane is not protecting DNA from ribosomes; it is keeping the mRNA away from them until modification is complete.

Transcription takes place in the nucleus and translation in the cytoplasm. Because the nuclear membrane separates the two, post-transcriptional modification of mRNA can happen before the mRNA meets ribosomes, which is the advantage the guide identifies.
A student who treats the eukaryotic pathway as universal picks this. In prokaryotes there is no nucleus, mRNA may meet ribosomes immediately, and modification before translation is not possible.

mcqs.q: A gene from a eukaryote is inserted into a bacterium and is transcribed there. In the eukaryotic cell the mRNA from this gene would be modified before translation. What happens to the mRNA in the bacterium?
options: It is modified in the cytoplasm before ribosomes can bind it.
It is translated inside the nucleoid before it is released.
It is not translated, as bacterial ribosomes read the DNA.
It is translated at once, without any modification.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why keep the nucleus and cytoplasm apart
mcqs.explain: In prokaryotes there is no nuclear membrane separating transcription from translation, so mRNA may immediately meet ribosomes and be translated, even while it is still being transcribed. Post-transcriptional modification is not possible.
rationales: A student who assumes every cell modifies mRNA before translation picks this. A bacterium has no nucleus to hold the mRNA apart from ribosomes, so there is no stage at which modification could happen first.

A student who thinks translation happens where the DNA is, inside a nucleus or its equivalent, picks this. The nucleoid is not a compartment; bacterial ribosomes are in the cytoplasm and bind the mRNA as it is transcribed.
A student who thinks ribosomes can translate DNA directly picks this. Ribosomes in all cells translate mRNA; in a bacterium the mRNA is translated as soon as ribosomes can attach to it.

In prokaryotes there is no nuclear membrane separating transcription from translation, so mRNA may immediately meet ribosomes and be translated, even while it is still being transcribed. Post-transcriptional modification is not possible.

mcqs.q: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes at a concentration far higher than in the surrounding cytoplasm. Why is keeping these enzymes inside a lysosome an advantage to the cell?
options: The enzymes are concentrated where they are needed and kept apart from the cytoplasm, whose contents they would otherwise hydrolyse.
The membrane merely stores the enzymes, since their specificity would stop them harming the cell if they escaped.
The membrane slows hydrolysis to a safe rate by limiting how fast substrates can reach the enzymes inside.
The lysosome is where the enzymes are synthesised, so they have to be kept in the organelle that made them.
mcqs.explain: This is the double advantage of compartmentalization the guide names: concentration of enzymes and metabolites, and separation of incompatible biochemical processes. Hydrolysis of macromolecules is incompatible with the rest of the cytoplasm.
rationales: This is the double advantage of compartmentalization the guide names: concentration of enzymes and metabolites, and separation of incompatible biochemical processes. Hydrolysis of macromolecules is incompatible with the rest of the cytoplasm.

A student who reads enzyme specificity as 'acts only on its intended target' picks this. Lysosomal enzymes are specific to bond types found in every protein, lipid and nucleic acid in the cell, so their escape would be destructive.
A student who sees a compartment as a brake on metabolism picks this. Concentrating enzymes and substrates in a small volume speeds reactions up; the membrane's role is separation, not slowing.
A student who slides from 'contains enzymes' to 'makes enzymes' picks this. Lysosomes have no ribosomes; their enzymes are made on the rough ER and delivered by the Golgi apparatus.

mcqs.q: A phagocyte engulfs a bacterium into a phagocytic vacuole, and lysosomes then fuse with the vacuole. What is the advantage of digesting the bacterium inside this compartment rather than in the cytoplasm?
options: The enzymes could safely be released anywhere in the cell, so the vacuole serves only to hold the bacterium still.
Hydrolytic enzymes reach a high concentration around the bacterium while being unable to digest the phagocyte's own contents.
The vacuole makes its own enzymes on its membrane, so the lysosomes only add more membrane to enlarge it.
Digestion in the cytoplasm would be too rapid to control, so the vacuole membrane slows the enzymes' access to the bacterium inside.
mcqs.explain: Fusion delivers the lysosomal enzymes into the small volume of the vacuole, so they act on the bacterium at high concentration, and the vacuole membrane separates this incompatible process from the rest of the cytoplasm. Both advantages of compartmentalization apply.
rationales: A student who believes enzyme specificity makes lysosomal enzymes harmless picks this. Released into the cytoplasm they would hydrolyse the phagocyte's own proteins and membranes; the vacuole keeps that process separate.

Fusion delivers the lysosomal enzymes into the small volume of the vacuole, so they act on the bacterium at high concentration, and the vacuole membrane separates this incompatible process from the rest of the cytoplasm. Both advantages of compartmentalization apply.

A student who thinks vacuoles produce digestive enzymes picks this. A phagocytic vacuole has no enzymes of its own; it is the fusion of lysosomes that supplies them, which is the whole point of the fusion.
A student who thinks membranes exist to slow processes down picks this. The compartment speeds digestion by concentrating enzyme and substrate together; it does not throttle it.

mcqs.q: During aerobic cell respiration the electron transport chain pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space of the mitochondrion. Why is the small volume of the intermembrane space an adaptation for ATP production?
options: Its volume is not itself an adaptation: it is the total number of protons stored that determines the ATP yield.
It brings oxygen entering through the outer membrane close to the cristae, which absorb it for use in respiration.
Few protons need to be pumped to produce a steep concentration gradient, so the gradient forms quickly.
It stops enzymes from the cytoplasm getting in and interfering with the electron transport chain.
mcqs.specStatementText: How a mitochondrion is built for ATP (HL)
mcqs.explain: Concentration is number of particles per unit volume. Pumping protons into a small volume raises their concentration sharply, so a steep gradient across the inner membrane is established rapidly and ATP synthase can begin working sooner.
rationales: A student who treats the space as a proton reservoir picks this. Chemiosmosis is driven by the concentration gradient across the inner membrane, and a small volume is what allows a steep gradient to form from few protons.

A student who explains every mitochondrial feature in terms of absorption picks this. Oxygen diffuses freely through both membranes; the intermembrane space is an adaptation for proton accumulation, not for oxygen uptake.

Concentration is number of particles per unit volume. Pumping protons into a small volume raises their concentration sharply, so a steep gradient across the inner membrane is established rapidly and ATP synthase can begin working sooner.

A student who reads the double membrane as protection picks this. The outer membrane, not the size of the space, sets what enters, and the space's small volume matters because of its effect on proton concentration.

mcqs.q: Electron micrographs of mitochondria from two tissues were analysed. In tissue X the inner membrane had an area of about 40 µm² per µm³ of mitochondrial volume; in tissue Y the value was about 15 µm² per µm³. Which conclusion is best supported by these data?
options: Mitochondria in tissue X absorb oxygen and glucose more quickly through their more extensive cristae.
Mitochondria in tissue X carry out the Krebs cycle faster, since it takes place on the cristae.
Mitochondria in tissue Y store more protons, because a smaller inner membrane leaves a larger intermembrane space.
Mitochondria in tissue X hold more electron transport chains and ATP synthase per unit volume.
mcqs.specStatementText: How a mitochondrion is built for ATP (HL)
mcqs.explain: The inner membrane, folded into cristae, is where the electron transport chain and ATP synthase are located. More inner membrane area per unit volume means more of these complexes, so a higher capacity for ATP production; this is what the data directly support.
rationales: A student who links surface area only to absorption picks this. Cristae are folds of the inner membrane and do not increase the area for uptake into the organelle; their area matters for the processes located in the inner membrane.
A student who assigns every mitochondrial process to the cristae picks this. The Krebs cycle takes place in the matrix; the inner membrane holds the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.

A student who thinks a bigger proton store is the aim picks this. The data say nothing about the volume of the intermembrane space, and in any case a small space is the adaptation, because it lets a steep gradient form quickly.

The inner membrane, folded into cristae, is where the electron transport chain and ATP synthase are located. More inner membrane area per unit volume means more of these complexes, so a higher capacity for ATP production; this is what the data directly support.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly matches an adaptation of the chloroplast to its function in photosynthesis?
options: The thylakoid membranes provide a large surface area in which photosystems are held to absorb light.
The fluid inside the thylakoids contains the enzymes of the Calvin cycle at high concentration.
The stroma holds the photosystems in solution so that light can reach them from every direction.
The thylakoids enclose a large volume of water to act as the substrate for photolysis.
mcqs.specStatementText: How a chloroplast is built for photosynthesis (HL)
mcqs.explain: Photosystems are embedded in the thylakoid membranes, and the large total area of these membranes allows many photosystems to be packed into the chloroplast, an adaptation the guide names explicitly.
rationales: Photosystems are embedded in the thylakoid membranes, and the large total area of these membranes allows many photosystems to be packed into the chloroplast, an adaptation the guide names explicitly.

A student who places every stage of photosynthesis in the thylakoids picks this. The Calvin cycle enzymes and substrates are compartmentalized in the stroma; the thylakoid space is where protons accumulate.
A student who pictures chlorophyll dissolved in fluid picks this. Photosystems are pigment-protein complexes embedded in the thylakoid membranes, not dissolved in the stroma.

A student who reads the thylakoid as a water tank picks this. The volume of fluid inside a thylakoid is small, which lets a proton gradient build up quickly; water is available throughout the chloroplast.

mcqs.q: Both mitochondria and chloroplasts produce ATP by chemiosmosis. Which feature of the chloroplast plays the same role as the small intermembrane space of the mitochondrion?
options: The large volume of water held inside the thylakoids, which supplies the protons released by photolysis.
The small volume of fluid inside each thylakoid, in which protons accumulate to form a steep gradient quickly.
The stroma, in which the photosystems pump protons into the surrounding fluid of the chloroplast.
The space between the two membranes of the chloroplast envelope, where protons are stored until they are needed.
mcqs.specStatementText: How a chloroplast is built for photosynthesis (HL)
mcqs.explain: In the chloroplast, protons are moved into the thylakoid space; its small volume means their concentration rises rapidly, giving a steep gradient across the thylakoid membrane for ATP synthase, exactly as the small intermembrane space does in the mitochondrion.
rationales: A student who thinks the thylakoids store water picks this. The thylakoid space is small, not large, and that smallness is the adaptation; water is not stored there.

In the chloroplast, protons are moved into the thylakoid space; its small volume means their concentration rises rapidly, giving a steep gradient across the thylakoid membrane for ATP synthase, exactly as the small intermembrane space does in the mitochondrion.
A student who places the photosystems in the stroma picks this. Photosystems are in the thylakoid membranes, and protons are moved into the thylakoid space, not into the stroma.

A student who sees the intermembrane space as a proton store, and looks for the matching store in the chloroplast, picks this. The chloroplast's proton gradient is across the thylakoid membrane, not across the envelope.

mcqs.q: A cell is treated with a substance that blocks all of its nuclear pores. Which consequence would follow?
options: DNA could no longer leave the nucleus to be translated by the ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
Protein synthesis would carry on, as ribosomes inside the nucleus would translate the mRNA there.
mRNA could no longer leave the nucleus, so cytoplasmic ribosomes would receive no new mRNA.
mRNA and proteins would still cross the envelope, diffusing through its bilayers as small molecules do.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why the nucleus has a double membrane with pores (HL)
mcqs.explain: The nuclear pores are the only route for mRNA and ribosomal subunits out of the nucleus and for proteins such as polymerases into it. Blocking them cuts off the supply of new mRNA to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm, which is why the double membrane needs pores.
rationales: A student who thinks DNA travels to the ribosomes picks this. DNA never leaves the nucleus; it is mRNA transcribed from the DNA that passes out through the pores.
A student who places translation in the nucleus picks this. There are no functional ribosomes in the nucleus, so mRNA that cannot leave cannot be translated.

The nuclear pores are the only route for mRNA and ribosomal subunits out of the nucleus and for proteins such as polymerases into it. Blocking them cuts off the supply of new mRNA to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm, which is why the double membrane needs pores.

A student who assumes anything can diffuse across a membrane picks this. Large polar molecules such as RNA and proteins cannot cross phospholipid bilayers, which is precisely why the nuclear envelope must have pores.

mcqs.q: What happens to the nuclear membrane during mitosis, and why?
options: It pinches into two so that each daughter nucleus keeps part of the original envelope.
It opens its pores wider so that the chromosomes can pass out into the cytoplasm.
It stays intact throughout, because the chromosomes can diffuse through its two bilayers.
It breaks into vesicles so that spindle microtubules can reach the chromosomes.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why the nucleus has a double membrane with pores (HL)
mcqs.explain: Spindle microtubules form in the cytoplasm. The nuclear membrane breaks into vesicles during mitosis and meiosis so that the microtubules can attach to the chromosomes and move them; the envelope re-forms from vesicles around each daughter nucleus.
rationales: A student who pictures the nucleus dividing like a cell picks this. An intact envelope would keep the spindle microtubules away from the chromosomes, so the envelope must break down, not pinch.

A student who thinks the pores are a route for genetic material picks this. Chromosomes do not pass through pores; the envelope disassembles into vesicles and reassembles around each set of chromosomes.

A student who thinks anything can diffuse across a membrane picks this. Chromosomes are far too large to cross a bilayer, and it is the spindle that must reach them, which requires the envelope to break down.

Spindle microtubules form in the cytoplasm. The nuclear membrane breaks into vesicles during mitosis and meiosis so that the microtubules can attach to the chromosomes and move them; the envelope re-forms from vesicles around each daughter nucleus.

mcqs.q: A pancreatic cell makes the digestive enzyme trypsinogen, which it secretes, and the enzyme hexokinase, which catalyses the first step of glycolysis in its cytoplasm. Where are the two proteins synthesised?
options: Trypsinogen on ribosomes bound to the rough endoplasmic reticulum; hexokinase on free ribosomes lying in the cytoplasm.
Trypsinogen on free ribosomes, which can move to the plasma membrane; hexokinase on the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
Both on the rough endoplasmic reticulum, from which the hexokinase is later released into the cytoplasm.
Trypsinogen in the Golgi apparatus, which makes secreted proteins; hexokinase on free ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
mcqs.specStatementText: Free ribosomes and the rough ER (HL)
mcqs.explain: Proteins for secretion are made on membrane-bound ribosomes on the rough ER and enter its lumen for transport via the Golgi apparatus. Proteins retained in the cell, such as a glycolytic enzyme, are made on free ribosomes and released into the cytoplasm.
rationales: Proteins for secretion are made on membrane-bound ribosomes on the rough ER and enter its lumen for transport via the Golgi apparatus. Proteins retained in the cell, such as a glycolytic enzyme, are made on free ribosomes and released into the cytoplasm.

A student who reads 'free' as 'free to travel' picks this. Free ribosomes make proteins that stay in the cell; secreted proteins are made on ribosomes bound to the rough ER, which is the reverse of this option.
A student who thinks all protein synthesis happens on the rough ER picks this. Proteins made on the rough ER enter its lumen; a cytoplasmic enzyme is made on a free ribosome and never enters the ER.
A student who thinks the Golgi apparatus makes secreted proteins picks this. The Golgi apparatus has no ribosomes; it processes and packages trypsinogen made on the rough ER.

mcqs.q: Pancreatic cells were supplied with radioactive amino acids for 3 minutes and then with non-radioactive amino acids. Samples of cells were taken at intervals and the location of radioactive protein was found. After 5 minutes it was mainly in the rough endoplasmic reticulum, after 20 minutes mainly in the Golgi apparatus, and after 60 minutes mainly in vesicles close to the plasma membrane. Which conclusion do these results support?
options: Protein flows along a continuous membrane channel from the rough ER, through the Golgi apparatus, to the plasma membrane.
Protein made on the rough ER is passed to the Golgi apparatus for processing and then packaged into secretory vesicles.
The Golgi apparatus synthesises the secreted protein, using amino acids that it receives from the rough ER.
The vesicles near the plasma membrane will be expelled whole from the cell, carrying the protein out with them.
mcqs.specStatementText: The Golgi apparatus processes and packages (HL)
mcqs.explain: Radioactive protein appears first where it is synthesised, on the rough ER, then in the Golgi apparatus, then in vesicles that will fuse with the plasma membrane. This is the sequence of processing and secretion of protein that the guide specifies for the Golgi apparatus.
rationales: A student who pictures the organelles as joined picks this. The label moves between separate organelles in discrete steps and ends in vesicles; the ER and Golgi apparatus are not continuous, and vesicles carry protein between them.

Radioactive protein appears first where it is synthesised, on the rough ER, then in the Golgi apparatus, then in vesicles that will fuse with the plasma membrane. This is the sequence of processing and secretion of protein that the guide specifies for the Golgi apparatus.

A student who thinks the Golgi apparatus makes protein picks this. The label is already in protein in the rough ER at 5 minutes, before any appears in the Golgi apparatus, so synthesis happened on the ER.

A student who thinks exocytosis pushes the vesicle out picks this. The data show where the protein is, not how it leaves; in exocytosis the vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane and only the contents are released.

mcqs.q: What is the role of clathrin in the formation of a vesicle?
options: It lines the inside of the vesicle so that it can bind and hold the cargo molecules that are being transported.
It is the membrane receptor protein that recognises and binds the substance that is to be brought into the cell.
It assembles into a lattice on the cytoplasmic side of the membrane, bending it into a pit that pinches off.
It builds a new membrane around the cargo, separate from the existing membrane, to enclose it.
mcqs.explain: Clathrin molecules assemble into a cage-like lattice beneath the membrane, which forces the membrane to curve inwards into a coated pit; the pit pinches off as a vesicle, and the clathrin coat is then removed.
rationales: A student who reads 'coat' as a lining picks this. Clathrin is on the cytoplasmic face of the membrane, never in contact with the cargo, and is shed once the vesicle has formed.
A student who confuses clathrin with the receptor picks this. Recognition is done by separate receptor proteins in the membrane; clathrin's role is structural.

Clathrin molecules assemble into a cage-like lattice beneath the membrane, which forces the membrane to curve inwards into a coated pit; the pit pinches off as a vesicle, and the clathrin coat is then removed.
A student who thinks vesicles are made from scratch picks this. A vesicle is a bud of existing membrane; clathrin shapes that membrane, it does not construct a new one.

mcqs.q: A vesicle from the Golgi apparatus carries a protein to the plasma membrane for secretion. What happens to the membrane of the vesicle when the protein is released?
options: It passes out through the plasma membrane and is lost from the cell.
It is broken down into phospholipids reused to build the next vesicle.
It stays joined to the Golgi apparatus as a channel for more protein.
It fuses with the plasma membrane and becomes part of it.
mcqs.explain: In exocytosis the vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane, releasing the contents outside the cell. The vesicle's phospholipids and proteins are added to the plasma membrane, which is also how the membrane of a growing cell is enlarged.
rationales: A student who pictures the vesicle popping out of the cell picks this. A vesicle cannot pass through a membrane; its bilayer fuses with the plasma membrane and only the contents leave.

A student who thinks vesicle membranes are built and dismantled picks this. Membrane is transferred, not destroyed: the vesicle's bilayer joins the plasma membrane, and new vesicles bud from existing membranes.
A student who imagines continuous channels between organelles picks this. A vesicle is a separate, detached compartment; it buds from the Golgi apparatus and later fuses with the plasma membrane.

In exocytosis the vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane, releasing the contents outside the cell. The vesicle's phospholipids and proteins are added to the plasma membrane, which is also how the membrane of a growing cell is enlarged.

mcqs.q: The enzymes and substrates of the Krebs cycle are held together in the mitochondrial matrix rather than being spread through the cytoplasm. Why is this compartmentalization an adaptation for the production of ATP?
options: The matrix holds the Krebs cycle enzymes pressed tightly against the cristae, so that they can pump protons directly into the intermembrane space.
Enzymes and substrates are concentrated in a small volume, so reactions run rapidly, and reduced NAD is formed close to the inner membrane.
Being enclosed by two membranes protects the Krebs cycle enzymes from being damaged by substances in the rest of the cytoplasm.
The inner membrane slows the entry of substrates into the matrix, so that the Krebs cycle runs at a safe and controlled rate.
mcqs.specStatementText: How a mitochondrion is built for ATP (HL)
mcqs.explain: Compartmentalizing the Krebs cycle in the matrix keeps enzymes and metabolites at high concentration, increasing reaction rate, and places the source of reduced NAD next to the inner membrane where it is oxidized. This is the third adaptation named in the guide for B2.2.4.
rationales: A student who assigns every mitochondrial process to the cristae picks this. The Krebs cycle is a series of reactions in solution in the matrix; proton pumping is done by the electron transport chain in the inner membrane, not by Krebs cycle enzymes.

Compartmentalizing the Krebs cycle in the matrix keeps enzymes and metabolites at high concentration, increasing reaction rate, and places the source of reduced NAD next to the inner membrane where it is oxidized. This is the third adaptation named in the guide for B2.2.4.

A student who reads the double membrane as protection picks this. The membranes create compartments in which concentration gradients and concentrated enzyme-substrate mixtures can be maintained; protection is not the adaptation.

A student who thinks compartments exist to slow metabolism picks this. Concentrating enzymes and substrates together speeds the cycle; transport proteins in the inner membrane supply substrates rather than throttling them.

mcqs.q: In a chloroplast the enzymes of the Calvin cycle are located in the stroma, while ATP and reduced NADP are produced by the thylakoid membranes. Why is locating the Calvin cycle in the stroma an adaptation for photosynthesis?
options: The Calvin cycle actually takes place inside the thylakoids themselves, and the stroma serves only to store the carbohydrate that the cycle produces.
The stroma holds the photosystems in solution, so the Calvin cycle enzymes must be located there too in order to receive light energy directly.
Enzymes and substrates are concentrated together in the stroma, next to the thylakoids that supply ATP and reduced NADP, so fixation is rapid.
The stroma provides the large volume of water that the thylakoid membranes need for the photolysis of water in the light.
mcqs.specStatementText: How a chloroplast is built for photosynthesis (HL)
mcqs.explain: Compartmentalization of the Calvin cycle enzymes and substrates in the stroma keeps them at high concentration and next to the thylakoid membranes that supply ATP and reduced NADP. This is the third adaptation named in the guide for B2.2.5.
rationales: A student who places every stage of photosynthesis in the thylakoids picks this. The light-dependent reactions are in the thylakoid membranes; the Calvin cycle is a series of enzyme-catalysed reactions in solution in the stroma.

A student who pictures chlorophyll dissolved in fluid picks this. Photosystems are embedded in the thylakoid membranes; the Calvin cycle does not use light directly but the ATP and reduced NADP made by the thylakoids.

Compartmentalization of the Calvin cycle enzymes and substrates in the stroma keeps them at high concentration and next to the thylakoid membranes that supply ATP and reduced NADP. This is the third adaptation named in the guide for B2.2.5.

A student who thinks the chloroplast's compartments are water stores picks this. Water is abundant throughout the chloroplast; the stroma's role in this adaptation is to concentrate the Calvin cycle enzymes and substrates.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: The only advantage of the nucleus tested is that transcription in the nucleus is kept apart from translation in the cytoplasm, so mRNA can be modified before it meets ribosomes, and that prokaryotes cannot do this. Nothing is included on protection of DNA, on regulation of gene expression by controlling nuclear import and export, or on the detailed mechanisms of intron removal, capping and polyadenylation, which belong to other topics.

The Golgi apparatus is treated only as the organelle that receives protein from the rough endoplasmic reticulum in vesicles, processes it and packages it into vesicles for secretion. Nothing is included on the naming of cis, medial and trans cisternae, on lipid processing, or on the synthesis of cell wall polysaccharides in plants. The origin of lysosomal enzymes is mentioned only in m12 and a q05 distractor rationale, as background, and is never tested as a key.
